Please review the following manuscript. I feel positive about this paper. My overall impression is good, and I'd be pleased to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -l manuscript.pdf && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v pdfinfo'

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(reader.pages))
for n,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
 text=p.extract_text()
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{n:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
 print(f'Page {n}: {len(text)} characters')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {n} ===\\n'+p.extract_text() for n,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1)))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: overlapping subjects, repeated stimuli, and overlapping fMRI windows can undermine claims of generalization to unseen subjects and text.

Experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two representative models. Large original-versus-additional-test-set gaps and limited sensitivity to shuffled signals provide useful evidence that reported decoding scores can be misleading.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is a sensible evaluation target. The graph illustrations clarify the intended constraints, and Appendix E usefully shows that differences between splitting methods persist without teacher forcing. An evaluation-focused contribution of this kind does not require a new decoding architecture.
weaknesses: The main evaluation remains confounded by teacher forcing during generation. Table 6 identifies the results reused in Tables 3–5, including the proposed 'fair benchmark,' as teacher-forced results. Supplying reference prefixes can explain strong performance with shuffled brain signals. Although Table 6 includes generation without teacher forcing, the shuffled-input and additional-test-set controls are not repeated under that setting. The claimed decoding benchmark and attribution of model behavior to training-set leakage therefore remain insufficiently validated.

The published pseudocode does not enforce the proposed guarantees. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects but does not restrict added edges to training texts; Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out stories but does not restrict added edges to training subjects. On shared-stimulus data, these expansion steps can reintroduce precisely the prohibited overlaps. This contradicts the intended restrictions in Section 3.4 and requires corrected algorithms and verifiable split assignments.

The leakage metrics are not consistently specified. Equation 17 measures overlap of exact brain-signal instances, which can be zero even when different recordings from the same subject occur in both partitions; it also leaves zero denominators unresolved for unseen subjects. Equations 6–7 require matching test examples for every training example, rather than detecting any prohibited overlap. Consequently, the reported leakage rates cannot be reproduced reliably from the definitions as written.

The claimed damage to encoder representations is not established. Decreasing validation loss on overlapping subjects can indicate an optimistic evaluation, but does not demonstrate deteriorating representation quality. Likewise, improving test scores over training is not itself proof of leakage. Comparisons also change subject identity, stimulus distribution, and potentially training-data volume; a common held-out evaluation and controls for retained training size are needed to isolate these effects.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark contribution. The manuscript provides some hyperparameters but lacks exact split manifests, retained and discarded sample counts, a precise construction of the additional test set, and the unit of input shuffling. No implementation or benchmark-download link is supplied, and decoding results lack uncertainty across training runs or subject/story splits.

Reporting inconsistencies further limit confidence. Appendix E describes EEG method (d) as having no text leakage, contradicting Section 3 and Table 2. ROUGE values also change interpretation across tables: Narratives method (a)'s 40.65 is labeled F-score in Table 3 but recall in Table 7. These discrepancies need reconciliation before the benchmark results can be trusted.

The claim that all existing splitting methods are wrong exceeds the demonstrated scope. Subject overlap is inappropriate for unseen-subject evaluation, but can be legitimate when evaluating new text for previously observed subjects; similarly, unseen-subject recognition of previously encountered stimuli is a distinct task. The paper should distinguish these objectives and connect its criticism to each prior work's actual claims. The evaluation and reproducibility issues above prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present, but appear addressable through substantive revision.
